claims.text: Replacing LPBF with room-temperature ink-extrusion printing followed by sintering will substantially reduce residual thermal stresses in AlCrFeNiSi miniature components.
The proposed process will improve the mechanical properties of AlCrFeNiSi components relative to LPBF.
The starting AlCrFeNiSi powder is pre-alloyed and gas-atomized.
Ink-extrusion printing can form the green part at room temperature.
Binder removal followed by sintering at 1200–1400 °C under an inert or reducing atmosphere is an applicable processing route for AlCrFeNiSi.
The process is applicable to miniature components with feature sizes below 10 mm.
Controlled-atmosphere sintering can produce homogeneous densification.
Reduced thermal gradients during processing lead to lower residual stresses.
Reduced thermal gradients produce a more homogeneous microstructure.
The proposed route produces fewer rapid-solidification-induced defects than LPBF.
Room-temperature ink printing minimizes rapid local melting and cooling and therefore reduces thermal shock and stress accumulation.
Controlled sintering permits gradual densification and microstructural refinement without the high thermal gradients characteristic of LPBF.
Ink-extruded and sintered AlCrFeNiSi components will have higher yield strength than LPBF components.
Ink-extruded and sintered AlCrFeNiSi components will have higher hardness than LPBF components.
Ink-extruded and sintered AlCrFeNiSi components will have higher ductility than LPBF components.
Conventional LPBF-produced AlCrFeNiSi components suffer from high residual thermal stresses.
Rapid melting and cooling during LPBF degrade the mechanical properties of AlCrFeNiSi components.
Process success depends sensitively on binder formulation and precise sintering parameters.
Scalability of the process to larger parts remains unestablished.
Failure to obtain statistically significant residual-stress reductions and improved mechanical performance relative to matched LPBF controls would falsify the hypothesis.
